topic: What to Say During a Traffic Stop to Protect Your Rights
strongest_angle: Most people lose their rights during traffic stops not because they're guilty, but because they don't know the four specific lines that constitutional lawyers have refined over decades of litigation — and they say too much in a moment where every word becomes evidence

key_facts.fact: Four-line script refined over decades of civil-rights litigation: (1) I do not consent to any searches. (2) Am I being detained, or am I free to go? (3) I am exercising my right to remain silent. (4) I would like to speak to a lawyer.
The classic opener 'Do you know why I pulled you over?' is a trick question — no matter how you answer, it could be used against you. You are under no obligation to provide an admission.
A routine traffic stop is NOT considered 'custody' for Miranda purposes. Officers can ask questions at the roadside without reading you your rights, and your answers are still admissible in court.
Police are permitted to lie about evidence, witnesses, fingerprints, and even DNA matches during questioning. The only defense is to make no statement that depends on the truth of what they say.
The Innocence Project has documented over 375 DNA exonerations, and roughly 30% involved false confessions or statements extracted from people who thought talking would clear them.

Rodriguez v. United States (2015): police cannot extend a traffic stop — even briefly — to conduct a K-9 sniff or other investigation unrelated to the stop's original mission without independent reasonable suspicion.

As of July 2025, 32 jurisdictions across 16 states have limited or eliminated non-safety-related traffic stops. Research shows police who stopped enforcing non-safety violations were MORE effective at addressing drunk driving and speeding.

People who experience frequent police stops are significantly more likely to develop symptoms of anxiety and PTSD — even youth who witness stops without being stopped themselves report higher depression and lower happiness.

You MUST verbally invoke your silence. The Supreme Court held in Salinas v. Texas (2013) that silence alone can be used against you — you must explicitly say 'I am exercising my right to remain silent.'

Recording the encounter is your First Amendment right. Courts consistently hold that police officers acting in public duties have no reasonable expectation of privacy. A recording once produced a $70,000 settlement in a wrongful DUI case.
